lines.text: The police can search your car without a warrant — and they have for a hundred years. But there's one place they still can't follow it.

It goes back to 1925 and a Prohibition bootlegger named Carroll. Agents tore open his seats and found sixty-eight bottles of whisky — no warrant. The Court said a car isn't a house: it can be driven off before a warrant is ever signed. So with probable cause, police can search it on the spot.

But probable cause is the catch. Being pulled over isn't permission, and a hunch isn't enough — an officer needs a real, specific reason. And the search only reaches where the thing they're after could fit. Chasing a stolen television doesn't let them open a pill bottle.

Then came Virginia. An officer walked up a driveway, lifted a tarp off a motorcycle he believed was stolen, and confirmed it. In 2018, by eight to one, the Supreme Court said no. The driveway hugging your home is curtilage — part of the house — and the car-search power stops there. It extends, the Court said, no further than the car itself.
